projects.title: Sable & Salt
projects.summary: A coastal restaurant group asked for an identity that could survive salt, sun and a crowded table. We built a system around a single drawn rule that re-draws itself on every surface it lands on.

body.alt: Sable & Salt identity — drawn rule across a warm ground
body.caption: The rule: one stroke, redrawn per surface.

body.text: A line that keeps its nerve

The owners had already tried three identities that photographed beautifully and aged badly. The brief was less romantic: be legible at three metres, in low light, next to a busy table, and still be recognisable when printed on a paper bag that would be soaked within the hour.

We answered with a drawn rule — a single hairline that stretches, contracts and doubles according to the surface it sits on. On the menu it is a divider. On the awning it is a horizon. On the door it becomes the handle.

body.alt: Sable & Salt menu system in close detail
body.caption: Menu system, uncoated stock, single ink.

body.text: The first time a customer drew the line in the air to show a colleague where the table was, we knew the mark was working.

body.caption: Signage study, dusk, west elevation.

projects.title: Northern Light Reclamation
projects.summary: A foundation that funds the restoration of northern industrial sites needed a name, a mark and a building-sized wayfinding language that could hold its own against the landscapes it sits in.

body.alt: Northern Light Reclamation identity on a cold ground
body.caption: The mark: a horizon that is also a section drawing.

body.text: Building a mark that behaves like daylight

Every previous identity we saw for institutions like this one tried to be monumental. Ours is the opposite: the mark is a horizon line that changes with the hour, drawn from the measured angle of light at the four sites the foundation restores.

On paper it is a rule. On screen it is a gradient that runs from the site's winter light to its midsummer light. On the building it is cut into the steel, and it is only ever as wide as the room it names.

body.alt: Wayfinding panels for the Northern Light Foundation
body.caption: Wayfinding: the line becomes a threshold.

body.text: They handed us a brand that changes with the season. That is not a metaphor here — the sites are 900 kilometres apart and the light is not the same.

body.caption: Site: light data drives the identity.

projects.title: Kite
projects.summary: A small studio making household objects out of agricultural waste asked for a name that could carry a product line without sounding like a product line.

body.alt: Kite packaging system in green and clay
body.caption: One box, six products.

body.text: A name that floats
The studio was making trays, bowls and brushes from flax and potato waste. The name had to be short, warm and slightly impossible to picture — a shape you can hold in the mind without seeing it.
The identity is deliberately quiet: a single word set large, a rule that indicates the material content of the box, and a colour that is mixed from the waste stream of that production run.

body.caption: Labels print the batch colour, not a swatch.

body.text: It is the first identity I have seen that gets out of the way of the object.

body.caption: Spring range, photographed in the studio.

projects.title: The Long Room
projects.disciplines: Book design, Type system, Print production
projects.summary: A quarterly of long-form essays printed on a single sheet that folds once. We designed a grid that works at four sizes and a masthead that stays out of the way of the text.

body.alt: The Long Room cover in clay and black
body.caption: Issue 14, folded sheet.

body.text: One fold, four sizes

The press publishes essays that run to forty pages. The sheet is folded once, so every spread has to be designed in the knowledge that it will be read flat, folded, and read again in a different configuration.
We drew a single grid in two columns and let the type do the rest. The masthead is set in the same face as the body, one size up, tracked out until it becomes a line rather than a word.

body.caption: Interior: the fold is part of the grid.

body.text: Readers write in to tell us which essay they read first and which they read second. We have stopped trying to predict it.

body.caption: Print run, four hundred sheets.

projects.title: Field Notes on Concrete
projects.summary: A research body publishing field notes on concrete published eleven volumes in four years. We gave them an identity that behaves like a filing system, not a magazine.

body.alt: Field Notes on Concrete volumes lined up
body.caption: Eleven volumes, one spine rule.

body.text: A filing system that happens to be a magazine
The Bureau measures concrete for a living: slump, strength, curing, carbon. Their notes were precise, plain and completely un-designed. The brief was to keep the precision and lose the inattention.

Each volume carries the same structural frame, and the only thing that changes from cover to cover is a single measured value printed at a size proportional to its magnitude. Volume seven is lighter than volume three because its aggregate was.

body.caption: Data plates: one value, one scale.

body.text: For the first time the shelf looks like the archive actually is — a set of measurements, not a set of opinions.
body.cite: Dr. Yusuf Adeyemi — Bureau of Structures

body.alt: Field Notes index and specimen pages
body.caption: Specimen pages, uncoated, single colour.

projects.title: Meltwater
projects.summary: A label releasing ambient records asked for an identity that could sit behind a sleeve, a stage backdrop and a streaming player without ever becoming the picture.

body.alt: Meltwater label mark in dusk violet
body.caption: The mark: a gradient that never repeats.

body.text: A mark that recedes

The label's whole proposition is that the music is the event and the sleeve is the receipt. So the identity is deliberately quiet: one gradient, one rule, and a catalogue number that is treated as the real logo.
Each release inherits a gradient generated from the recording's own waveform envelope, so no two sleeves in the catalogue are alike and none of them compete with the music.

body.caption: Sleeve series, catalogue MW-014 to MW-021.

body.text: We stopped designing covers and started printing data. The fans noticed the numbers before they noticed the colours.

body.caption: Stage backdrop, 12 × 4 metres.

projects.title: Halcyon Type Foundry
projects.summary: A foundry releasing its first family needed a name, an identity and a specimen that could be read as a specimen — not as an advertisement for a specimen.

body.alt: Halcyon type specimen in rust and cream
body.caption: Specimen cover, rust ink on cream.

body.text: A foundry that behaves like a library

Halcyon's argument is that a type foundry should be a shelf, not a showroom. The identity borrows from library cataloguing: a classification number, a spine, and a typographic hierarchy strict enough to file anything.

The first family — a high-contrast serif for long reading — ships with a variable weight axis and an optical size axis, and every specimen is generated from the live font so nothing is ever a picture of the type.

body.caption: Specimen interior: the family, at nine sizes.

body.text: They gave us an identity that is basically a good index. We are unreasonably pleased about it.

body.caption: Specimen wall, Rotterdam.

projects.title: Ordinary Objects, Carefully
projects.summary: An exhibition of everyday domestic objects needed a title that did not flatter them. The identity had to survive being printed on a wall, a card and a receipt.

body.caption: Wall graphics: a list, set as a list.

body.text: A catalogue that behaves like a catalogue
Two hundred and eleven objects: a chipped cup, a doormat, a bus ticket. The exhibition wanted no glamour and no irony, which is a much harder thing to design than either.
We used a single column, a single size, and the object list itself as the graphic device. The title sets the tone: everything, including the typography, is treated with the same care as the objects.

body.caption: Catalogue: 320 pages, no images.

body.text: Visitors kept asking whether the wall text was part of the exhibition. It was, and that was the point.

body.caption: Receipt cards, printed on the spot.

projects.title: Vesper
projects.summary: A three-person architecture practice that wanted to be judged on its drawings rather than its photographs, and asked for an identity with no imagery at all.

body.alt: Vesper identity drawn in sand and black
body.caption: Identity: a drawn section, nothing else.

body.text: No photographs
Vesper's work is drawings. Their competitors' work is photographs. The brief was to build a site with no images at all — only plans, sections, and the occasional sentence.
The identity is a single drawn line that marks the cut of every section it accompanies, and the website scrolls like a roll of drawings, one sheet at a time.

body.caption: The site scrolls as a roll of drawings.

body.text: They made us look like the practice we actually are, which is slower and better.

body.caption: Drawing set, issued quarterly.
